source_text: Quamquam ista quaestio uires intellegentiae meae uincit, quemadmodum opitulentur martyres his, quos per eos certum est adiuuari: utrum ipsi per se ipsos adsint uno tempore tam diuersis locis et tanta inter se longinquitate discretis, siue ubi sunt eorum memoriae siue praeter suas memorias, ubicumque adesse sentiuntur, an ipsis in loco suis meritis congruo ab omni mortalium conuersatione remotis et tamen generaliter orantibus pro indigentia supplicantum — sicut nos oramus pro mortuis, quibus utique non praesentamur nec ubi sint uel quid agant scimus — deus omnipotens, qui est ubique praesens nec concretus nobis nec remotus a nobis. exaudiens martyrum preces, per angelica ministeria usquequaque diffusa praebeat hominibus ista solacia, quibus in huius uitae miseria iudicat esse praebenda, et suorum martyrum merita ubi uult, quando uult, quomodo uult, maximeque per eorum memorias, quoniam hoc nouit expedire nobis ad aedificandam fidem Christi, pro cuius illi confessione sunt passi, mirabili atque ineffabili potestate ac bonitate commendet. res est haec altior, quam ut a me possit adtingi, et abstrusior, quam ut a me ualeat perscrutari. et ideo quid horum duorum sit, an uero fortassis utrumque sit, ut aliquando ista fiant per ipsam praesentiam martyrum, aliquando per angelos suscipientes personam martyrum, definire non audeo. mallem ab scientibus ista perquirere. neque enim nemo est, qui haec sciat, non qui sibi scire uideatur et nesciat. dona enim dei sunt his alia et illis alia largientis secundum apostolum, qui dicit unicuique dari manifestationem spiritus ad utilitatem. alii quidem, inquit, datur per spiritum sermo sapientiae; alii sermo scientiae secundum eundem spiritum; alteri autem fides in eodem spiritu; alii donatio curationum in uno spiritu; alii operationes uirtutum; alii prophetia; alii diiudicatio spirituum; alii genera linguarum; alii interpretatio sermonum: omnia autem haec operatur unus atque idem spiritus diuidens propria unicuique prout uult. horum omnium spiritalium donorum, quae commemorauit apostolus, cuicumque data est diiudicatio spirituum, ipse scit ista sicut scienda sunt.
thought_title: How martyrs help the living surpasses my understanding
orientation: Augustine has just argued that the dead cannot by nature be involved in the affairs of the living, and now he turns to the question of how martyrs nevertheless help the living.
pass_a_gloss: Although this question overcomes the powers of my understanding, in what way martyrs help those who it is certain are helped through them: whether they themselves through themselves are present at one time in so many different places and places separated by so great a distance from one another, either where their memorial shrines are or besides their own memorial shrines, wherever they are sensed to be present, or whether, they themselves being in a place suited to their merits, removed from all converse with mortals, and yet generally praying for the needs of those who pray — just as we pray for the dead, to whom we are certainly not presented, nor do we know where they are or what they do — God almighty, who is present everywhere and neither joined to us nor removed from us, hearing the prayers of the martyrs, through angelic ministries spread everywhere, provides to human beings those comforts which he judges should be provided in the misery of this life, and commends the merits of his martyrs where he wills, when he wills, how he wills, and especially through their memorial shrines, because he knows this is expedient for us for building up the faith of Christ, for whose confession they suffered, with wonderful and ineffable power and goodness. This matter is higher than that it can be reached by me, and more hidden than that it can be searched out by me. And therefore which of these two it is, or whether perhaps it is both, so that sometimes these things happen through the very presence of the martyrs, sometimes through angels taking up the person of the martyrs, I do not dare to define. I would prefer to inquire about these things from those who know. For it is not that there is no one who knows these things, not one who seems to himself to know and does not know. For the gifts of God are, to some these and to others those, of him who bestows according to the apostle, who says that to each one is given the manifestation of the spirit for usefulness. To one indeed, he says, is given through the spirit a word of wisdom; to another a word of knowledge according to the same spirit; to another faith in the same spirit; to another the gift of healings in one spirit; to another workings of powers; to another prophecy; to another discernment of spirits; to another kinds of tongues; to another interpretation of speeches: but all these things one and the same spirit works, dividing to each one his own as he wills. Of all these spiritual gifts, which the apostle mentioned, to whomever discernment of spirits has been given, he himself knows these things as they should be known.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'memorial shrine' for memoria, and here it refers to the physical shrines at burial places of martyrs.
The passive of praesento means to be made present or brought into someone's presence; Augustine is saying the living praying for the dead are not made present to them.
Persona here means the role or identity that angels take up, representing the martyrs; 'person' preserves the Latin sense of identity or role.
This is the standard English rendering of the Pauline gift listed in 1 Corinthians 12:10, and Augustine is quoting that list.
Sermo here is the utterance or word given by the Spirit, matching the standard English of 1 Corinthians 12:8.
This renders the Pauline phrase literally; uirtutes here are miraculous powers or deeds of power.

bible_refs.note: unicuique dari manifestationem spiritus ad utilitatem ... alii quidem datur per spiritum sermo sapientiae ... omnia autem haec operatur unus atque idem spiritus diuidens propria unicuique prout uult

pass_b_english: Yet this question goes beyond the strength of my understanding: how martyrs help those who are certainly aided through them. Do they themselves, by their own power, attend at one time in places so diverse and separated by such great distances—whether where their memorial shrines are, or apart from their shrines, wherever they are felt to be present? Or are they themselves in a place suited to their merits, removed from all dealings with mortals, and yet praying in a general way for the needs of those who entreat them—just as we pray for the dead, though we are certainly not present to them, nor do we know where they are or what they are doing—and does almighty God, who is present everywhere and neither joined to us nor far from us, hear the prayers of the martyrs and, through angelic ministries spread everywhere, provide to human beings those comforts that he judges should be provided in the misery of this life? And does he commend the merits of his martyrs where he wills, when he wills, how he wills—and especially through their memorial shrines, because he knows this helps us to build up faith in Christ, for whose confession they suffered—by his wonderful and ineffable power and goodness? This matter is too high for me to reach, and too hidden for me to search out. And so I do not dare to define which of these two it is, or whether perhaps it is both—that sometimes these things happen through the very presence of the martyrs, sometimes through angels taking on the role of the martyrs. I would rather ask those who know. For it is not that there is no one who knows these things—not someone who merely seems to himself to know yet does not know. These are gifts of God, who gives one thing to some and another to others, according to the apostle, who says that to each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good. "To one," he says, "is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom; to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit; to another gifts of healings in the one Spirit; to another workings of powers; to another prophecy; to another discernment of spirits; to another kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation of utterances. All these are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each one his own as he wills" (1 Corinthians 12:8-11). Of all these spiritual gifts that the apostle listed, whoever has been given discernment of spirits knows these things as they ought to be known.

problems.quote: who merely seems to himself to know and does not know
problems.source_quote: non qui sibi scire uideatur et nesciat
problems.why: Negation misread: 'non nemo est, qui haec sciat, non qui...' means 'there is someone who knows, not someone who merely seems...'
problems.fix: For there is someone who knows these things, not someone who merely seems to himself to know yet does not know.

problems.why: Augustine's quotation begins at verse 8 ('alii quidem...'), not verse 7; verse 7 is 'unicuique datur manifestatio spiritus'
problems.ruling: Augustine's quote starts at 'alii quidem' (v.8); v.7 ('unicuique datur') is paraphrased, not quoted, so citing 12:7-11 misleads.

edits.old: For there is no one who knows these things who merely seems to himself to know and does not know.
edits.new: For there is someone who knows these things, not someone who merely seems to himself to know yet does not know.

fixed: Mistranslation of 'non nemo est, qui haec sciat, non qui sibi scire uideatur et nesciat': the double negation means 'there is someone who knows, not someone who merely seems to know'; corrected.
Scripture citation: Augustine's quotation begins at verse 8 ('alii quidem...'), not verse 7; corrected to 1 Corinthians 12:8-11.

problems.quote: For there is someone who knows these things, not someone who merely seems to himself to know yet does not know.
problems.source_quote: neque enim nemo est, qui haec sciat, non qui sibi scire uideatur et nesciat.
problems.why: Latin says 'there is no one who does NOT know' = everyone knows; English says 'there is someone who knows'.
problems.fix: For there is no one who knows these things who does not truly know them, unlike one who merely seems to himself to know yet does not know.
problems.ruling: Latin 'neque enim nemo est, qui haec sciat' = 'for there is no one who does not know this' (litotes: everyone knows). English inverts to 'there is someone who knows,' weakening universal claim.

edits.old: For there is someone who knows these things, not someone who merely seems to himself to know yet does not know.
edits.new: For it is not that there is no one who knows these things—not someone who merely seems to himself to know yet does not know.

fixed: Negation: source 'neque enim nemo est, qui haec sciat, non qui sibi scire uideatur et nesciat' means 'For it is not that there is no one who knows these things—not one who seems to himself to know and does not know.' The English 'there is someone who knows' lost the double negation; restored it.

problems.quote: taking up the person of the martyrs
problems.why: "Personam" here means role/character, not individual person; angels assume the martyrs' role/identity.
problems.fix: angels taking on the role of the martyrs

problems.quote: And does he commend the merits of his martyrs
problems.why: 'Commendet' is jussive subjunctive continuing from 'praebeat': 'let him commend,' not a question.
problems.fix: And let him commend the merits of his martyrs
problems.ruling: 'commendet' is jussive subjunctive parallel to 'praebeat,' not interrogative; 'And let him commend' or 'commending' needed.

fixed.quote: we are certainly not presented to them
fixed.fix: we are certainly not present to them
fixed.note: 'praesentamur' means 'we are present to them'; 'presented to' is a calque that shifts the meaning.
'commendet' belongs with 'praebeat' in the same open question, not a wish; the sentence already ends in a question mark, so only the verb needs changing.
